_comment: Biomes. The campaign map's ground is data first, exactly as battlefield terrain is: the simulation reads a type and a movement number, the renderer reads a palette and a texture, and neither knows about the other. A BIOME is a look - a ground texture, a palette, a height character and a set of props. A TYPE (data/terrain/terrain_types.json) is a rule - how fast a soldier crosses it. Every biome names the type it behaves as, so adding a snowfield never changes a movement number, and re-balancing movement never changes how anything looks. When biomes meet, a tile carries WEIGHTS (70% grass, 30% forest) and colour, height, prop density and movement all read those weights.

_fields.id: stable key, used by the world generator and by battlefields
_fields.name: what a player would call it
_fields.type: the terrain_types.json id whose movement rule this biome follows
_fields.grounds: one to four res:// paths with a name and the dominant colour sampled from the art. The first is the default; the generator picks one per tile from a seeded hash of the tile's position, so a tile always shows the same one and neighbours rarely repeat. At a biome border, whichever variants the two tiles chose are what blend.
_fields.ground_scale: how many world units one repeat of a ground image covers (a knob: tune when it is on screen)
palette: two to four colours, darkest first: what the height shading darkens and lightens from when there is no ground image

props.density: props per 100 tiles at full weight
props.min_weight: how much of this biome a tile needs before the prop appears at all

biomes.name: Plains
biomes.notes: Four looks rather than four variations of one: Standard, Lush, Dry and Worn differ in colour and wear, so they can later be chosen by moisture, season or region instead of at random. Art is 1254x1254, top-down and painted; props to follow.
